q: The nucleus of an atom is made up of:
x: In the simple model of the atom, protons and neutrons (together called nucleons) form the nucleus, while electrons move around it outside the nucleus.

q: An alpha particle is identical to:
x: An alpha particle consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, i.e. a helium nucleus ⁴₂He, with charge +2e.

q: Nuclear radiation damages living cells mainly because it:
o: Ionises atoms and molecules in the cells, such as DNA
Heats the cells until they boil
Adds extra protons to the cell nuclei
x: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation knock electrons out of atoms. This ionisation breaks molecules such as DNA, which can kill cells or make them grow abnormally.

q: The atomic number Z of an element is the number of:
o: Protons plus electrons in its atom
x: Z is the number of protons (the charge number) of the nucleus. The total number of protons and neutrons is the mass number A.

q: Radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra) decays by emitting an alpha particle. The daughter nucleus is:
x: Alpha emission lowers A by 4 and Z by 2: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He.

q: A radioactive source widely used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells with gamma rays is:
x: Cobalt-60 emits strong gamma rays and is used to irradiate tumours. Carbon-14 is used in dating, and sodium-24 as a tracer for blood flow.

q: How many neutrons are there in a nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U?
x: Number of neutrons N = A − Z = 238 − 92 = 146. 238 is the total number of nucleons and 92 the number of protons.

q: When a nucleus emits a beta particle (an electron), its mass number and atomic number change as follows:
o: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2
A is unchanged and Z rises by 1
A is unchanged and Z falls by 1
A rises by 1 and Z is unchanged
x: In beta-minus decay a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is emitted. The nucleon number stays the same and Z increases by 1, e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N.

q: To check how well a patient's thyroid gland is working, a doctor gives a small amount of a radioactive tracer. A suitable tracer is:
x: The thyroid takes up iodine, so radioactive iodine-131 collects there and its radiation can be detected from outside to show how the gland is working.

q: Isotopes of an element have:
o: The same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
The same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
The same mass number but different atomic numbers
Different numbers of protons and electrons
x: Isotopes have the same atomic number Z (same element) but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ. Nuclei with the same A but different Z are isobars.

q: When a nucleus emits gamma radiation:
o: Neither its mass number nor its atomic number changes
x: Gamma rays are high-energy photons with no charge and no mass, so emitting them only lowers the energy of the nucleus; A and Z stay the same.

q: Gamma rays are used to sterilise sealed packs of syringes and surgical instruments because they:
o: Make the instruments radioactive, which kills germs later
Are stopped by the packaging, which keeps germs out
Penetrate the packaging and kill bacteria without heating the contents
Change the metal of the instruments into a germ-free isotope
x: Gamma rays pass through the sealed plastic and kill microorganisms. Items can be sterilised after packing and without heat, and they do not become radioactive.

q: Which pair of nuclei are isotopes of the same element?
x: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C both have Z = 6 but 6 and 8 neutrons. ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N have the same mass number but are different elements.

q: Which list puts the three radiations in order of DECREASING penetrating power?
x: Gamma rays are the most penetrating (need thick lead), beta particles are stopped by a few mm of aluminium, and alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper. The ionising order is the reverse.

q: The SI unit of absorbed dose, equal to 1 joule of radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue, is the:
x: Absorbed dose is measured in gray: 1 Gy = 1 J kg⁻¹. The becquerel and curie are units of activity; the sievert is used for equivalent dose, which also allows for the type of radiation.

q: A neutral atom of ³⁵₁₇Cl contains:
x: Z = 17 protons; N = 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons; a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, 17.

q: A beam containing alpha, beta and gamma radiation passes through an electric field. Which radiation passes through undeflected?
x: Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves, so electric and magnetic fields do not deflect them. Alpha (positive) and beta (negative) particles are deflected in opposite directions.

q: Damage caused by radiation to the reproductive cells of a person, which may appear in that person's children, is called a:
x: Genetic effects come from damage to the DNA of reproductive cells and can be passed to offspring. Somatic effects, such as burns or cancer, appear in the exposed person.

q: Different isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties because they have the same:
x: Chemical behaviour depends on the electrons. Isotopes have the same number of protons and so, as neutral atoms, the same number of electrons; only the neutron number and mass differ.

q: Radioactive decay is described as random. This means that:
o: The total number of decays per second can never be estimated
Each nucleus decays after the same fixed time
The nuclei decay one after another in a fixed order
It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or exactly when
x: Each nucleus has a certain chance of decaying in a given time, but we cannot say which one will decay or when. For a large number of nuclei the average rate can still be predicted, which is why half-life is useful.

q: Singly charged ions of neon-20 and neon-22 enter the same magnetic field of a mass spectrograph with the same speed. The neon-20 ions move on a circle of radius 10 cm. The radius for the neon-22 ions is:
x: r = mv/(qB), and q, v and B are the same, so r ∝ m: r = 10 × 22/20 = 11 cm. Inverting the ratio gives 9.1 cm, taking √(22/20) gives about 10.5 cm, and squaring it gives 12.1 cm.

q: The mass defect of a nucleus is:
o: The mass of the nucleus minus the mass of its protons
The mass of the electrons in the atom
The total mass of its separate protons and neutrons minus the mass of the nucleus
The mass lost when the nucleus emits an alpha particle
x: A nucleus has less mass than its free nucleons; the difference Δm = Zm_p + Nm_n − M is the mass defect, and Δm c² is the binding energy that holds the nucleus together.

q: A deuteron (²₁H nucleus) has a mass of 2.0136 u. The mass of a proton is 1.0073 u and of a neutron 1.0087 u. The mass defect of the deuteron is:
x: Δm = (1.0073 + 1.0087) − 2.0136 = 2.0160 − 2.0136 = 0.0024 u. Using two protons gives 2.0146 − 2.0136 = 0.0010 u; 0.0014 u is just the neutron-proton mass difference.

q: A helium-4 nucleus has a mass of 4.0015 u. Mass of proton = 1.0073 u, mass of neutron = 1.0087 u and 1 u = 931 MeV. The binding energy per nucleon of helium-4 is about:
x: Δm = 2(1.0073) + 2(1.0087) − 4.0015 = 4.0320 − 4.0015 = 0.0305 u, so binding energy = 0.0305 × 931 ≈ 28.4 MeV and per nucleon = 28.4/4 ≈ 7.1 MeV. 28.4 MeV is the total, and dividing by the 2 protons only gives 14.2 MeV.

q: On the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, the highest values (about 8.8 MeV per nucleon) occur for nuclei near:
x: Binding energy per nucleon rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks near iron-56 (about 8.8 MeV), then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV for uranium. So iron-group nuclei are the most stable, and both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones release energy.

q: The binding energy per nucleon of ²³⁸₉₂U is 7.6 MeV. Its total binding energy is about:
x: Total binding energy = A × (per nucleon) = 238 × 7.6 ≈ 1809 MeV. Multiplying by the 92 protons gives 699 MeV and by the 146 neutrons gives 1110 MeV; 31 MeV comes from dividing 238 by 7.6.

q: The mass defect of a nucleus is 2 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. Its binding energy is: (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: E = Δm c² = 2 × 10⁻²⁹ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 1.8 × 10⁻¹² J. Forgetting to square c gives 6 × 10⁻²¹ J, and putting in an extra ½ (as if kinetic energy) gives 9 × 10⁻¹³ J.

q: Four nuclei have these mass numbers and total binding energies. Which is the most stable?
o: A nucleus of 60 nucleons with 480 MeV
A nucleus of 200 nucleons with 1580 MeV
A nucleus of 20 nucleons with 150 MeV
A nucleus of 40 nucleons with 340 MeV
x: Stability is judged by binding energy per nucleon: 340/40 = 8.5, 480/60 = 8.0, 1580/200 = 7.9 and 150/20 = 7.5 MeV, so the 40-nucleon nucleus is most stable. Picking the largest total binding energy (1580 MeV) is the usual slip.

q: A heavy nucleus of 240 nucleons with binding energy 7.6 MeV per nucleon splits into two fragments of 120 nucleons each, with binding energy 8.5 MeV per nucleon. No free neutrons are produced. The energy released is about:
x: Energy released = gain in total binding energy = 240 × 8.5 − 240 × 7.6 = 240 × 0.9 = 216 MeV. 1824 MeV and 2040 MeV are the total binding energies before and after; counting only one fragment gives 108 MeV.

q: The activity of a radioactive sample falls from 800 Bq to 50 Bq in 20 hours. Its half-life is:
x: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 is 4 halvings, so 4 half-lives = 20 h and T½ = 5 h. Dividing 20 h by the factor 16 instead of by the number of half-lives gives 1.25 h.

q: A worker of mass 70 kg absorbs 0.14 J of energy from radiation spread through the whole body. The absorbed dose is:
x: Absorbed dose = energy/mass = 0.14/70 = 0.002 Gy = 2 mGy. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 9.8 Gy, and mass/energy gives 500 Gy.

q: In a Wilson cloud chamber, the tracks made by alpha particles are:
o: Long, faint and broken into scattered dots
x: Alpha particles are heavy and strongly ionising, so they leave dense, straight tracks of nearly equal length. Thin twisted tracks belong to light beta particles, and gamma rays give only faint scattered tracks from the electrons they eject.

q: In the reaction ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + X, the particle X is:
x: Mass numbers: 14 + 4 = 17 + A gives A = 1; atomic numbers: 7 + 2 = 8 + Z gives Z = 1. A particle with A = 1 and Z = 1 is a proton (¹₁H). A neutron would need Z = 0.

q: In the fission reaction ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n, the number x of neutrons released is:
x: Mass number on the left is 235 + 1 = 236; on the right 141 + 92 + x = 233 + x, so x = 3. Charge balances (92 = 56 + 36). Forgetting the incoming neutron gives 2.

q: The moderator in a thermal nuclear reactor, such as graphite or heavy water, is used to:
o: Absorb extra neutrons to stop the chain reaction
Carry heat from the core to the turbines
Slow down fast neutrons so they can cause more fissions of U-235
x: Fission neutrons are fast; collisions with light moderator nuclei slow them to thermal speeds, at which U-235 captures them far more readily. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods, which is the common mix-up.

q: Control rods in a nuclear reactor are usually made of cadmium or boron because these materials:
o: Slow neutrons down without absorbing them
x: Cadmium and boron capture neutrons, so pushing the rods in lowers the neutron number and the fission rate, and pulling them out raises it. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job, not the control rods'.

q: In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n, the masses are: ²₁H 2.0141 u, ³₂He 3.0160 u and neutron 1.0087 u. With 1 u = 931 MeV, the energy released is about:
x: Mass before = 2 × 2.0141 = 4.0282 u; after = 3.0160 + 1.0087 = 4.0247 u; Δm = 0.0035 u, so energy = 0.0035 × 931 ≈ 3.3 MeV. 1.6 MeV and 6.5 MeV are factor-of-2 slips (halving or doubling Δm), and 0.33 MeV is a decimal-place slip in 0.0035.

q: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei needs a temperature of millions of kelvin mainly because:
o: The nuclei must move fast enough to overcome their electrostatic repulsion
Heat is needed to split the nuclei first
Neutrons must be slowed down before fusion
High temperature increases the binding energy per nucleon
x: Both nuclei are positive, so they repel; only at very high temperatures do they have enough kinetic energy to come close enough for the strong nuclear force to join them. Slowing neutrons is relevant to fission, not fusion.

q: A fission reactor runs at a steady power when, on average, the number of neutrons from each fission that go on to cause another fission is:
x: If each fission leads to exactly one more fission, the chain reaction is critical and the fission rate is constant. Fewer than 1 makes the reaction die out; more than 1 makes it grow, as in a bomb. About 2-3 neutrons are released per fission, but most are lost or absorbed.

q: Each fission of U-235 releases 200 MeV. How many fissions per second are needed to produce 32 MW of power? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
x: 200 MeV = 200 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J, so the rate = 32 × 10⁶/3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ = 1 × 10¹⁸ per second. Treating 32 MW as 32 kW gives 1 × 10¹⁵; dividing 32 × 10⁶ by 200 without converting MeV gives 1.6 × 10⁵.
